final_proof:
Let
\[
G_0\xrightarrow{\phi_0}G_1\xrightarrow{\phi_1}G_2\xrightarrow{\phi_2}\cdots
\]
be the sequence of groups under consideration. For indices \(i\leq j\), write \(\phi_{i,j}:G_i\to G_j\) for the composite transition homomorphism, with \(\phi_{i,i}=\operatorname{id}_{G_i}\). Thus \(\phi_{j,k}\circ\phi_{i,j}=\phi_{i,k}\) whenever \(i\leq j\leq k\). Suppose that the homomorphisms \(h_i:G_i\to H\) are compatible with the transition maps; equivalently,
\[
h_j\circ\phi_{i,j}=h_i\qquad(i\leq j).
\]

Recall that the underlying set of \(G_\infty\) consists of equivalence classes of pairs \((x,i)\), where \(x\in G_i\), under the relation
\[
(x,i)\sim(y,j)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{there is some }k\geq i,j\text{ for which }
\phi_{i,k}(x)=\phi_{j,k}(y).
\]
The group law is computed at a common stage: for any \(k\geq i,j\),
\[
[(x,i)]\cdot[(y,j)]
=\bigl[(\phi_{i,k}(x)\phi_{j,k}(y),k)\bigr].
\]

Define
\[
h_\infty([(x,i)])=h_i(x).
\]
To prove that this is well-defined, suppose that \([(x,i)]=[(y,j)]\). By the definition of the equivalence relation, choose \(k\geq i,j\) such that \(\phi_{i,k}(x)=\phi_{j,k}(y)\). Compatibility gives
\[
h_i(x)=h_k(\phi_{i,k}(x))
=h_k(\phi_{j,k}(y))
=h_j(y).
\]
Hence the displayed value depends only on the equivalence class, so \(h_\infty\) is a well-defined mapping.

It remains to verify preservation of multiplication. Let \([(x,i)]),[(y,j)]\in G_\infty\), and choose any \(k\geq i,j\). Using the definition of the group law, the definition of \(h_\infty\), the fact that \(h_k\) is a homomorphism, and compatibility, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
h_\infty\bigl([(x,i)]\cdot[(y,j)]\bigr)
&=h_k\bigl(\phi_{i,k}(x)\phi_{j,k}(y)\bigr)\\
&=h_k(\phi_{i,k}(x))h_k(\phi_{j,k}(y))\\
&=h_i(x)h_j(y)\\
&=h_\infty([(x,i)])h_\infty([(y,j)]).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(h_\infty:G_\infty\to H\) is a well-defined group homomorphism.
